title: Listings in Quarto
text: Listings are Quarto’s built-in way to collect and display pages from a project. They are useful when a portfolio has multiple case studies, reflections, dashboards, or course projects that should be discoverable from one index page.

title: Listings in Quarto
text:
What a listing does
A listing reads metadata from matching documents and renders a collection of cards or rows. Each item can show a title, description, date, image, and category. The listing page becomes a reusable portfolio index instead of a manually maintained set of links.

title: Listings in Quarto
text:
A minimal listing configuration
listing:
  contents: projects
  type: grid
  fields: [image, title, description, date]
  sort: "date desc"
  categories: true
  filter-ui: true
The contents value points to a folder or pattern. type: grid creates a visual card layout, while categories and filter-ui help visitors narrow a larger collection.

title: Listings in Quarto
text:
Add metadata to each project
Each portfolio page can include front matter like this:
---
title: "Wellness Ranch SEO Audit"
description: "A research-led review of search visibility and conversion opportunities."
date: 2026-10-01
categories: [SEO, Analytics, Capstone]
image: images/seo-audit.png
---
The metadata becomes the content of the listing card. This is especially helpful for a portfolio because the summary can be written once and reused in navigation, search, and the project page.

title: Listings in Quarto
text:
Listing ideas for this portfolio


Case studies
Show the problem, approach, evidence, and outcome for client or class projects.


Reflections
Collect course reflections and explain what each project taught you.


Dashboards
Organize interactive reports, visualizations, and measurement frameworks.

title: Listings in Quarto
section: Why listings work well for a portfolio
text:
Why listings work well for a portfolio
Listings scale with the work. A new project only needs its own page and metadata; the index updates when the site is rendered. This keeps the homepage focused while giving visitors a structured way to browse deeper work.






NotePractical tip



Use consistent metadata across every project. A clear title, one-sentence description, date, category, and image create a more useful listing than a collection of pages with inconsistent labels.

title: Extending Quarto with CSS and SCSS
text: Quarto gives a website a strong structure out of the box. CSS and SCSS make that structure feel intentional: they control typography, spacing, color, responsive layouts, and small interaction details without changing the content itself.

title: Extending Quarto with CSS and SCSS
text:
The styling workflow
Quarto source → HTML structure → styles.css → browser presentation
The _quarto.yml file connects the site to styles.css with one line:
format:
  html:
    css: styles.css

title: Extending Quarto with CSS and SCSS
Extending Quarto with CSS and SCSS
Extending Quarto with CSS and SCSS
Extending Quarto with CSS and SCSS
text:
Accessibility considerations
Good styling should support access, not just appearance. Use sufficient color contrast, visible focus states, meaningful heading order, descriptive link text, and readable line lengths. Quarto handles much of the semantic structure; CSS should enhance it rather than hide it.

title: Extending Quarto with CSS and SCSS
text:
Why SCSS can help
SCSS adds nesting, variables, mixins, and partial files to CSS. For a small portfolio, plain CSS is enough. For a larger site, SCSS can organize theme tokens, components, and responsive rules into separate files before compiling them into one stylesheet.






TipTakeaway



Use Quarto for content and navigation, and use CSS or SCSS for the visual system. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the website easier to revise and publish.

title: Name of Assignment
text:
For this activity, I completed a YouGov survey and paid attention to questions that seemed unusual, confusing, or unrelated to what I expected from a survey. Some questions stood out because the answer choices were intentionally strange, while others made me wonder why the researchers wanted that information. Looking at these questions helped me think more carefully about how surveys are designed and how respondents may react to different types of questions.






YouGov question asking about activities completed during the previous weekend


The first question I chose to report asked:

“Which of the following activities did you do last weekend? Please select all that apply.”

I thought this question was weird because the list combined very normal activities with extremely unlikely or impossible activities. For example, “Brushed your teeth” and “Talked with family or friends” are common things that many people probably did. However, other choices included “Won a lifetime achievement award,” “Performed for an audience of 500,000+ people,” and “Discovered the lost city of Atlantis.”
At first, I did not understand why a survey would include such unrealistic choices. After thinking about it, I believe the question may have been designed as an attention check. A respondent who is carefully reading the question would probably select only activities that actually happened. Someone who is clicking through the survey without paying attention might select an obviously impossible answer.
This question showed me that surveys do not always ask questions only because the researchers want information about the topic itself. Sometimes a question may be included to evaluate the quality of the responses and determine whether participants are reading the survey carefully.






YouGov question asking for an opinion about beef jerky


The second question asked respondents to give their opinion about beef jerky, with the choices “Strongly like,” “Like,” “Dislike,” “Strongly dislike,” and “Not sure.”
I selected this question because it seemed very specific and somewhat random compared with the types of demographic, social, or political questions I normally associate with YouGov. I was curious about why researchers would need to know whether someone likes beef jerky.
Unlike the first example, the question itself was easy to understand. What confused me was its purpose. One possibility is that YouGov was collecting consumer-preference data that could later be used for market research. Companies may want to understand which groups of people like certain foods or products. It is also possible that responses to a question like this could be compared with demographic characteristics or other preferences.
This made me realize that a question can be simple for the participant but still have a research purpose that is not immediately obvious. Survey participants often see only individual questions, while the researcher may be looking for patterns across many different variables.



Completing the YouGov survey gave me several ideas that I can apply when designing my own research project.
First, I learned that every survey question should have a clear purpose. Even when the purpose is not obvious to the respondent, the researcher should know exactly why the question is included and how the response will be used in the analysis. Unnecessary questions can make a survey longer and may cause respondents to lose interest.
Second, I learned the importance of attention checks and response quality. The first YouGov example demonstrated one possible way to identify respondents who may not be reading carefully. In my own research, I should think about how I can make sure the data I collect are reliable. At the same time, attention checks should be written carefully so they do not unnecessarily confuse participants.
Third, I learned that response options need to be clear and complete. The beef jerky question provided several levels of opinion as well as a “Not sure” option. Providing an appropriate neutral or uncertainty option can be useful because respondents should not be forced to give an opinion when they do not have one.
Fourth, I learned that survey questions should make sense from the participant’s perspective. Researchers may understand why a question is important, but respondents do not always have that context. If questions seem completely random or unrelated, participants may become confused about the survey’s purpose. For my research project, I should organize questions logically and make transitions between different topics when necessary.
Finally, this experience taught me that good survey design involves more than simply writing questions. Researchers also need to think about participant attention, wording, answer choices, question order, data quality, and how each response will eventually contribute to answering the research question.
Overall, completing the YouGov survey helped me see survey design from the respondent’s point of view. When I create my own research project, I want my questions to be easy to understand, purposeful, and organized in a way that encourages participants to give thoughtful and accurate responses.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
text: For this assignment, I modified the Social Media Opinion Leader survey in Qualtrics. The major changes included creating a randomized experimental design, routing participants to different advertisement conditions, improving the measurement of social media usage, and making three additional improvements to the questionnaire.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
text: For this assignment, I modified the Social Media Opinion Leader survey in Qualtrics. The major changes included creating a randomized experimental design, routing participants to different advertisement conditions, improving the measurement of social media usage, and making three additional improvements to the questionnaire.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
text:
1. Survey Flow and Experimental Design
I modified the Survey Flow so that participants are randomly assigned to one of two experimental conditions. The two conditions are the social_media_review condition and the ads condition.
The randomization occurs near the beginning of the survey after the participant ID is assigned.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
text:
2. Random Assignment
I added a Randomizer to randomly assign participants to one of the two advertisement conditions.
The embedded data variable used for the experimental condition is Ad Type.
The two possible values are:

reviewer
ads


This setup allows participants to be randomly assigned to one of the two experimental conditions.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
text:
3. Branch Logic for Advertisement Conditions
After participants are randomly assigned to an Ad Type, I used Branch Logic to determine which advertisement block they receive.
Participants assigned to the reviewer condition are shown the social_media_review block.
Participants assigned to the ads condition are shown the ads block.

The DV block remains outside the two branches so that all participants answer the same dependent-variable questions after viewing their assigned advertisement.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
section: 4. Improving the Social Media Usage Question
text:
4. Improving the Social Media Usage Question
The original social media usage question measured overall social media use. This made it difficult to determine how much time a participant spends on each individual platform.
I revised the question so that respondents can select all of the social media platforms they use rather than selecting only one.
The revised question asks:

Which of the following social media platforms do you use? Select all that apply.

I also changed the question setting so that multiple responses can be selected.
A second question was then used to measure the amount of time respondents spend on each platform they selected.
I used the Carry Forward Choices function and selected Selected Choices from the previous social media platform question.

This allows the next question to display only the social media platforms that the respondent previously selected.
For example, if a respondent selects Instagram and Snapchat, the next question asks about their usage of Instagram and Snapchat rather than displaying every possible platform.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
text:
5. Additional Questionnaire Improvements
In addition to the experimental design and Carry Forward function, I reviewed the questionnaire and made three additional improvements.

Improvement 1: Rewording a Question
I revised the wording of one question to make it clearer and easier for respondents to understand.
The original wording was:

Please indicate the extent to which you would rely on the following to get recommendations from to purchase a product?

I revised the question to:

Please indicate the extent to which you would rely on each of the following sources when seeking recommendations about a product purchase.

The revised wording is clearer and more grammatically consistent.



Improvement 2: Rewording Response Choices
I revised the response choices for a question asking how often respondents purchase a product or service that a social media opinion leader posted about.
The original response choices were lengthy and somewhat difficult to compare.
I simplified and standardized the wording so that the choices were easier to read:

Never (0%)
Rarely (about 10%)
Occasionally (about 30%)
Sometimes (about 50%)
Often (about 70%)
Usually (about 90%)
Every time (100%)


This change makes the response scale more consistent and easier for respondents to understand.


Improvement 3: Adding an Additional Response Option
For my third improvement, I added an additional response option to a question where the original set of choices may not have represented every possible response.
Adding another response option gives respondents a more complete set of choices and reduces the chance that they will have to select an answer that does not accurately represent them.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
text:
6. Testing the Survey
After making the changes, I used Qualtrics Preview mode to test the survey multiple times.
I verified that:

Participants are assigned to only one advertisement condition.
Participants do not see both advertisement treatments.
The DV questions appear regardless of which advertisement condition is assigned.
The social media question allows respondents to select multiple platforms.
The Carry Forward question displays only the platforms selected in the previous question.

title: Qualtrics M02: Social Media Opinion Leader – Experimental Design
text:
Conclusion
The revised Qualtrics survey uses a between-subjects experimental design in which participants are randomly assigned to one of two advertisement conditions.
Branch Logic ensures that participants see only their assigned advertisement condition, while all participants subsequently answer the same dependent-variable questions.
The revised social media questions also provide more detailed information by allowing respondents to identify all platforms they use and report their usage for each platform separately.
Finally, three additional questionnaire improvements were made by improving question wording, simplifying response choices, and adding an additional response option.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
This reflection summarizes what I learned from the module on Quarto Revealjs presentations and advanced data wrangling in R.
For the presentation activity, I created a Revealjs slide deck based on my Capstone Experience Project, Wellness Ranch Therapy. The presentation focused on improving website visibility, search-engine optimization, digital advertising, analytics tracking, and meaningful conversions.
The reflection connects the presentation experience to advanced data-wrangling concepts, including relational joins, reshaping data, and grouped summaries.






NoteMain Takeaway



This module helped me understand that data analysis involves both technical and communication skills. Advanced data-wrangling functions help prepare the data, while Quarto helps explain the findings to an audience.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
2.1 Prompt

In Step 1, you learned how to design presentation slides with Quarto. What is your impression of the Revealjs presentation? Describe its capabilities as you learned from the presentations. What are its strengths and weaknesses compared with PowerPoint?

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
2.2 Response
My impression of Revealjs is that it is a flexible and reproducible way to create professional presentations using Markdown, Quarto, R, and HTML. Instead of creating each slide manually in a graphical presentation program, I can write the slide content in a .qmd file and render it into an interactive HTML presentation.
One of the most useful capabilities of Revealjs is that it allows text, code, tables, charts, citations, speaker notes, and links to be included in one source document. This is especially useful for data-analysis presentations because the charts and tables can be generated directly from the data.
Revealjs also supports several visual and interactive features, including:


Ready-made presentation themes
Slide transitions
Incremental lists
Fragments
Speaker notes
Slide numbers
Table of contents
Columns
Scrollable content
Footnotes
Internal slide links
Reproducible R code
Embedded resources
Custom CSS styling


Another strength is reproducibility. If the data changes, I can rerun the Quarto document and update the chart or table without manually editing the presentation. This reduces the possibility of copying an old number into a slide.
Revealjs also works well for presentations that need to be shared online. The final product is an HTML file that can be published on a website or through a service such as Quarto Pub.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
2.3 Strengths Compared with PowerPoint
Revealjs has several strengths compared with PowerPoint:



Table 1: Strengths of Revealjs compared with PowerPoint.









Revealjs strength
Explanation




Reproducibility
Code can automatically generate tables and charts


Transparency
The source file documents how the results were created


Web publishing
Presentations can be viewed in a browser


Version control
A text-based file is easier to compare and update


Flexible formatting
HTML and CSS allow detailed customization


Integration with R
Data analysis and presentation can exist together

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
2.4 Weaknesses Compared with PowerPoint
Revealjs also has limitations. PowerPoint can be easier for users who prefer dragging, resizing, and formatting objects visually. PowerPoint also provides familiar tools for animations, shapes, diagrams, and direct editing.
Revealjs requires more familiarity with Markdown, Quarto syntax, HTML, CSS, and sometimes R. A small syntax mistake can prevent the presentation from rendering correctly. It can also take additional time to learn how to control slide layouts and visual spacing.



Table 2: Limitations of Revealjs compared with PowerPoint.









Revealjs limitation
Explanation




Learning curve
Requires knowledge of Markdown and Quarto


Layout control
Some visual adjustments require CSS


Rendering errors
Syntax or code errors can affect the final output


Collaboration
Some users may prefer graphical editing


Offline editing
PowerPoint may be more convenient for quick manual changes






Overall, I do not see Revealjs as a complete replacement for PowerPoint in every situation. Instead, I see Revealjs as especially valuable for technical, analytical, and reproducible presentations. PowerPoint may be more convenient for presentations that depend heavily on manual design, animation, or graphical editing.

text:
3.5 What I Learned from Creating the Presentation
Creating the Revealjs presentation helped me understand the importance of storytelling in data analysis. I could not simply list digital-marketing concepts. I needed to organize the presentation around a business problem and a sequence of questions.
The presentation process helped me learn how to:


Convert a broad project topic into a central analytics question
Organize information into a logical slide sequence
Connect digital-marketing activities to measurable outcomes
Use code to create reproducible charts
Include speaker notes for additional explanations
Use columns and incremental lists to improve slide design
Add internal links to an appendix
Publish a presentation as a web-based HTML document


One challenge was deciding how much information to include on each slide. A technical report can contain more detail, but presentation slides should be concise enough for an audience to follow. I learned that slides should communicate the main idea while speaker notes or an appendix can provide additional detail.
I also learned that digital-marketing metrics need to be interpreted carefully. A website may receive many visitors, but traffic alone does not prove that the marketing strategy is successful. Meaningful outcomes may include contact-form submissions, phone calls, appointment requests, qualified inquiries, or other actions connected to the organization’s goals.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
4.2 Response
Advanced data wrangling allows an analyst to transform multiple datasets into a structure that can be analyzed and communicated. The three functions selected for this reflection are:

left_join() from the relational-data category
pivot_longer() from the data-reshaping category
summarise() from the grouped-summary category

These functions are useful for the Wellness Ranch Therapy project because digital-marketing information may be stored across multiple sources. Website traffic, advertising costs, campaign details, and conversion records may need to be combined before calculating performance measures.

title: M06-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Wrangling
text:
5.1 Category: Relational Data Joins

5.1.1 When to Use It
The left_join() function is used to combine two datasets using one or more matching keys. It keeps every row from the first dataset and adds matching information from the second dataset.
This would be useful for Wellness Ranch Therapy if one dataset contained campaign performance and another dataset contained campaign costs or campaign descriptions.
For example, the first dataset may contain channel-level performance information, while the second dataset contains marketing costs.


Code
channel_performance <- tibble(
  channel = c(
    "Organic Search",
    "Google Ads",
    "Social Media",
    "Email"
  ),
  conversions = c(32, 27, 12, 14)
)

channel_costs <- tibble(
  channel = c(
    "Organic Search",
    "Google Ads",
    "Social Media",
    "Email"
  ),
  marketing_cost = c(300, 950, 240, 120)
)

joined_channels <- channel_performance |>
  left_join(channel_costs, by = "channel")

joined_channels |>
  kable(
    caption = "Output from joining channel performance and marketing costs."

6.1 Category: Data Reshaping

6.1.1 When to Use It
The pivot_longer() function is used to convert data from a wide format into a long format.

text:
7.1 Category: Grouped Summaries

7.1.1 When to Use It
The summarise() function is used to calculate summary statistics such as totals, averages, counts, minimums, and maximums.
It is often used together with group_by(). The group_by() function identifies the groups, and summarise() calculates a result for each group.
For Wellness Ranch Therapy, this could be used to calculate total sessions, total conversions, and average conversion rates by channel.


Code
marketing_data <- tibble(
  channel = c(
    "Organic Search",
    "Organic Search",
    "Google Ads",
    "Google Ads",
    "Social Media",
    "Social Media"
  ),
  sessions = c(300, 320, 190, 220, 180, 175),
  conversions = c(15, 17, 12, 15, 6, 6)
)

channel_summary <- marketing_data |>
  group_by(channel) |>
  summarise(
    total_sessions = sum(sessions),
    total_conversions = sum(conversions),
    conversion_rate = total_conversions / total_sessions,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

channel_summary |>
  kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Grouped channel summary created with summarise()."
  )

text:
NoteDataset note



This report uses the pizzaplace dataset included with the gt package because CEP project data were not supplied with this assignment. The dataset is a synthetic, one-year pizza-sales dataset with 49,574 rows and seven variables, including order ID, date, pizza name, size, category, and price. It is suitable for demonstrating descriptive tables, grouping, and embedded mini-charts.

title: M05-Visualizing Data with Tables for MSDM CEP
section: 1 1. Prompt: What did you learn from the videos?
text:
1 1. Prompt: What did you learn from the videos?

1.1 Prompt
Summarize what you learned from the videos you watched.


1.2 Response
The videos showed that a table is not just a place to print a spreadsheet. With gt, a table can become a polished communication tool that combines a clear hierarchy, descriptive labels, formatted values, source notes, and visual emphasis. I learned to think about a table as a designed view of the data: first wrangle the information into the comparison I want, then use gt() to control how the result is communicated.
A second lesson was the value of small visualizations inside a table. The gtExtras package adds functions that can place sparklines, bars, distributions, and other compact graphics directly into table cells. For example, gt_plt_sparkline() converts a list-column of numeric values into a small trend graphic, while gt_plt_dist() can show a distribution in each row. This makes it possible to scan both numbers and patterns without switching between a chart and a separate table.
The broader lesson for data communication is to start with the question a reader needs answered. Formatting should support that question rather than decorate the output for its own sake.

title: M05-Visualizing Data with Tables for MSDM CEP
section: 2 2. Prompt: What did you like about the gt and gt and gtExtras packages?
text:
2 2. Prompt: What did you like about the gt and gt and gtExtras packages?

2.1 Prompt
What did you like about the gt and gt and gtExtras packages demonstrated in the videos?


2.2 Response
I liked the way the two packages work together. gt provides the table structure and precise formatting: titles, subtitles, labels, spanners, footnotes, source notes, number formats, and cell styling. gtExtras then extends that structure with compact plots, so the table can carry both exact values and visual signals in the same place. The result feels closer to a small dashboard or presentation-ready exhibit than a raw data frame.
I also like the reproducible workflow. Instead of manually formatting a table in a word processor or slide program, the table can be regenerated whenever the data change. That matters in an analytics project because the final exhibit remains connected to the analysis code.






TipDesign principle



Use formatting to make the intended comparison easier to see. A reader should not have to decode the table before finding the answer.

title: M05-Visualizing Data with Tables for MSDM CEP
section: 3 3. Prompt: How do tables complement charts?
text:
3 3. Prompt: How do tables complement charts?

3.1 Prompt
How do tables complement charts for data visualization?


3.2 Response
Tables and charts answer related but different questions. A chart is efficient for seeing patterns such as ranking, change over time, differences in magnitude, or unusual observations. A table is better for recovering the exact values behind those patterns. In other words, the chart supports pattern recognition, while the table supports precise lookup and comparison.
Using both can reduce the weaknesses of either format alone. For example, a chart may show that one pizza category generates more revenue than another, while a table can report the exact revenue, number of pizzas sold, average order value, and percentage of total revenue. A table with an embedded sparkline goes one step further by combining the exact number with a quick visual cue in the same exhibit.

title: M05-Visualizing Data with Tables for MSDM CEP
section: 4 4. Prompt: When would you prefer tables rather than charts?
text:
4 4. Prompt: When would you prefer tables rather than charts?

4.1 Prompt
Under what circumstances would you prefer to use tables rather than charts to visualize data?


4.2 Response
I would prefer a table when the audience needs exact values, when several metrics need to be compared across the same groups, or when the number of categories is large enough that a chart becomes difficult to read. Tables are especially useful for reporting KPIs, financial figures, rates, counts, or other values that a reader may need to quote or use in a later decision.
I would also choose a table when the differences are small and exact numbers matter more than a broad visual impression. A chart is usually more effective when the primary question is about shape, trend, or distribution; a table becomes more useful when the primary question is “What exactly is the value?”

title: M05-Visualizing Data with Tables for MSDM CEP
section: 5 5. Prompt: Use the MSDM CEP data (or pizzaplace) to create a descriptive table
text:
5 5. Prompt: Use the MSDM CEP data (or pizzaplace) to create a descriptive table

5.1 Prompt
Use the data for your MSDM CEP. If you don’t have data yet, use the pizzaplace dataset. Pick variables relevant to your Analytics Objectives and share descriptive statistics using gt and gtExtra functions together to show numbers and small charts in one table. Incorporate titles, a stub-head label, relabeled variable names, source notes, footnotes, a spanner column label, two-decimal formatting, currency signs where applicable, and visual emphasis.


5.2 Response: Analytics objective for the demonstration
For this demonstration, the practical analytics objective is: compare pizza categories on sales volume and revenue contribution while also showing whether revenue is consistently distributed across the year.
The table below groups the sales data by pizza category. It reports total pizzas sold, total revenue, average selling price, revenue share, and a compact monthly revenue sparkline. The combination is intended to answer both magnitude questions and trend questions in one place.


Code
pizza_table <- pizza_summary %>%
  gt(rowname_col = "type") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Pizza Category Performance**"),
    subtitle = md("Annual sales volume, revenue contribution, pricing, and monthly revenue trend")
  ) %>%
  tab_stubhead(label = "Pizza Category") %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Sales & Revenue",
    columns = c(pizzas_sold, revenue, revenue_share)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Pricing & Trend",
    columns = c(avg_price, monthly_revenue)
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    pizzas_sold = "Pizzas Sold",
    revenue = "Revenue",
    revenue_share = "Revenue Share",
    avg_price = "Avg. Selling Price",
    monthly_revenue = "Monthly Revenue Trend"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(pizzas_sold),
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  fmt_currency(
    columns = c(revenue, avg_price),
    currency = "USD",
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  fmt_percent(
    columns = revenue_share,
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  gt_plt_sparkline(
    column = monthly_revenue,
    type = "ref_mean",
    same_limit = TRUE,
    label = FALSE
  ) %>%
  data_color(
    columns = revenue,
    colors = scales::col_numeric(
      palette = c("#F2F2F2", "#2C7FB8"),
      domain = NULL
    )
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Revenue share is each category's share of total dataset revenue.",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = revenue_share)
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Sparkline shows monthly revenue; the reference line indicates the category's mean monthly revenue.",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = monthly_revenue)
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: gt package, pizzaplace built-in dataset."
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Note: Values are descriptive statistics for the assignment demonstration and are not intended to represent the user's final CEP dataset."
  ) %>%
  opt_row_striping() %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    data_row.padding = px(7)
  )

This table is worth adding because it turns several related KPIs into a single presentation-ready exhibit. 7 7. Prompt: Apply Quarto features that improve the HTML report

7.1 Prompt
Implement as many HTML features as possible, including text formatting, headings, lists, blockquotes, tabsets/tables, cross-referencing, footnotes, callouts, table of contents, toc-depth/toc-expand, section numbering, self-contained output, HTML theme options, hiding code, code overflow, and code tools.


7.2 Response
This report intentionally uses a range of Quarto features rather than treating the QMD as a plain script. The YAML enables automatic section numbering, a navigable table of contents, code linking, code tools, folded code, wrapped code overflow, and embedded resources for a self-contained HTML file. These are native Quarto HTML options.
The report also uses:

Headings and subheadings to separate each assignment prompt from its response.
Bold and italic text for emphasis.
Lists for scan-friendly explanations.
Blockquotes for the customer-oriented framing.
A panel tabset for a compact design explanation.
A cross-reference to Table Table 1.
Footnotes and table footnotes to explain definitions without interrupting the main text. See [^1] for an example.
Callout blocks to distinguish important notes, tips, and interpretation reminders.
A self-contained HTML configuration through embed-resources: true.
Code hiding and code tools so readers can focus on the report while still being able to inspect the analysis.







NoteWhy self-contained HTML matters



With embed-resources: true, Quarto can package linked images, styles, scripts, and other page resources into the HTML itself, reducing the need to carry a companion _files directory when the report is shared.

Establishes the “why” of the project: what real-world managerial issue motivates the study.
Should be specific, actionable, and framed so it can be translated into a research question.

Project Objectives (PO’s)

Broad statements describing the overall purpose/intent of the project.
Answer: What is the project trying to accomplish, at a high level?

Analytics Objectives (AO’s)

Narrower, measurable objectives that operationalize the PO’s.
Bridge between the managerial problem and specific research questions/hypotheses (this connects directly to W05-1).

Significance of the Project

Why the project matters — theoretical contribution, managerial/practical implications, or both.






Group Presentation & Peer Review

Each group presents their project introduction (problem statement, PO’s, AO’s, significance).
Peers provide structured feedback (clarity of problem, feasibility, alignment between PO’s/AO’s).

Note Taking with Quarto

Practice using .qmd files for structured, reproducible note-taking.
Use headers (#, ##, ###), bullet lists, and callout blocks to organize content.
Render to HTML/PDF to check formatting.

3 W05-2 — M07: Measurement & Scaling

3.1 Fundamentals and Comparative Scaling (Ch. 9)

Four Types of Scales

Nominal — categories only, no order (e.g., gender, brand names).
Ordinal — ranked categories, unequal intervals (e.g., satisfaction rank).
Interval — ordered, equal intervals, no true zero (e.g., Likert scales, temperature °F).
Ratio — ordered, equal intervals, true zero point (e.g., age, income, sales).

Comparative Scaling

Respondents directly compare objects against one another (e.g., paired comparison, rank order, constant sum).
Produces relative/ordinal data — good for competitive comparisons, less generalizable beyond the objects compared.








Important



Quiz for Ch. 9 (Assigned) — Due 9/24




3.2 Noncomparative Scaling Techniques (Ch. 10)

Continuous vs. Itemized Scales

Continuous (graphic) rating scale: respondents mark a point along a continuous line.
Itemized rating scale: respondents choose from a limited number of ordered categories (e.g., 5-point Likert).

Reliability & Validity

Reliability — consistency of measurement (test-retest, internal consistency/Cronbach’s alpha, alternative forms).
Validity — whether the scale measures what it’s intended to measure (content, criterion, construct validity).

4 W05-3 — SEM01: Measurement Model – Theory (1)

4.1 Test of Multi-Item Scales

Regression vs. SEM

Regression: tests relationships between observed variables; single equation, no explicit measurement error modeling.
SEM: tests relationships among latent constructs while simultaneously modeling measurement error; combines factor analysis + path analysis.




4.2 Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA)

Conducted with software (e.g., IBM SPSS).
Used to uncover underlying factor structure among a set of observed items before confirmatory testing.



4.3 Covariance-Based SEM (CB-SEM)

Conducted with software (e.g., IBM AMOS).
Two-step approach:

Measurement Model Testing

Reliability — internal consistency of indicators for each latent construct.
Validity

Convergent Validity — indicators of the same construct correlate highly (e.g., AVE, factor loadings).
Discriminant Validity — constructs are empirically distinct from one another (e.g., AVE vs. squared correlations).


Structural Model Testing

Test of Hypotheses — path coefficients between latent constructs are evaluated for significance and direction.





4.4 Articles

Anderson & Gerbing (1988) — foundational article on the two-step SEM approach (measurement model → structural model).

SEM01 – Take Notes for Anderson & Gerbing (1988)

5 W05-4 — Qualtrics M02: Setting Up an Experimental Design (Assigned)

Random Assignment

Randomly assigning respondents to different conditions/treatment groups to reduce bias and support causal inference.

Branching

Directing respondents down different survey paths based on their prior responses.

Experimental Design

Structuring manipulated conditions (IVs) within the survey to test causal effects on outcomes (DVs).

Piped Text

Dynamically inserting a respondent’s earlier answer (or other data) into later questions for personalization/consistency.

Carryover

Carryover (order) effects — when exposure to earlier questions/conditions influences responses to later ones; addressed via randomization/counterbalancing.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
Anderson and Gerbing (1988) argue that structural equation modeling (SEM) is often used carelessly, and they offer practical guidance for applying it more rigorously.
Their central recommendation is a two-step approach: first evaluate the measurement model (how observed indicators relate to latent constructs), and only then evaluate the structural model (how the constructs relate to one another).
The motivation is diagnostic. If a researcher estimates everything at once and the model fits poorly, it is unclear whether the problem lies in the measurement of the constructs or in the hypothesized theoretical relationships.
The article reviews estimation options, the logic of confirmatory measurement models, fit assessment, and respecification. It then explains why the two-step approach is preferable to a one-step approach and closes with cautions about interpreting structural results.
Main takeaway: separating measurement from structure produces clearer, more defensible conclusions about both the constructs and the theory.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
2.1 Exploratory Versus Confirmatory Analyses

Exploratory analysis (such as exploratory factor analysis) is used to discover or generate structure when theory is limited. Confirmatory analysis tests a structure that the researcher specified in advance.
SEM is fundamentally a confirmatory tool: the researcher states which indicators load on which constructs and which constructs are related, then checks whether the data are consistent with that specification.
In practice, researchers often drift into exploratory use by repeatedly modifying a poorly fitting model until it fits. The authors treat this as a serious concern because it capitalizes on chance features of the sample.
Any model that has been substantially modified using the same data should be treated as exploratory, and ideally tested again on new data (see the Respecification section).

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
section: 2.2 Complementary Approaches for Theory Testing Versus Predictive Application
text:
2.2 Complementary Approaches for Theory Testing Versus Predictive Application

The authors distinguish two research goals that call for different tools.

Theory testing and development: the aim is to assess whether a theoretical structure is consistent with the data, with attention to construct meaning and parameter estimates. Covariance-based SEM (for example, LISREL-type maximum likelihood) suits this goal.
Prediction: the aim is to explain variance in outcome variables. Approaches such as partial least squares (PLS) and regression-based methods are oriented toward this goal.

The two approaches are complementary rather than competitors. The right choice depends on whether the goal is to test a theory or to predict outcomes.
Because this article is about theory testing, its recommendations are framed around covariance-based SEM with latent variables.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
2.3 Estimation Methods

The article discusses the common estimation methods: maximum likelihood (ML), generalized least squares (GLS), unweighted least squares, and asymptotically distribution-free (ADF/WLS) methods.
ML and GLS assume multivariate normality but appear reasonably robust to moderate departures from it under adequate sample sizes.
ADF methods relax the normality assumption but need very large samples to perform well, which limits their practical use.
Sample size matters for stable estimates, convergence, and trustworthy fit tests. The authors point to simulation research suggesting that a few hundred cases or fewer can suffice for ML and GLS in well-specified models. 
Improper solutions (such as negative error variances) can arise from misspecification, small samples, or too few indicators per construct, and they should be investigated rather than ignored.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
3.1 Need for Unidimensional Measurement

Unidimensionality means each set of indicators measures a single underlying construct. It is a precondition for giving a latent variable a clear theoretical meaning.
If indicators reflect more than one dimension, the meaning of the construct becomes ambiguous and structural coefficients become hard to interpret.
The authors discuss two criteria.

Internal consistency: indicators of the same construct relate to each other in a way consistent with one common factor.
External consistency: an indicator’s relationships with indicators of other constructs are consistent with the model (for example, no unmodeled cross-loadings).

Coefficient alpha alone does not establish unidimensionality, so confirmatory factor analysis is preferred as a stricter test.
The authors generally advise against freeing correlated measurement errors to improve fit, since such correlations undermine unidimensionality and are hard to justify theoretically. They also tend to reflect sample-specific chance.
Well-specified measurement is what makes convergent validity (indicators of the same construct agree) and discriminant validity (different constructs are empirically distinct) testable.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
3.2 Specification

Specification means stating, before estimation, which indicators load on which factors, which loadings and error variances are free, and how the factors are allowed to relate (typically all freely correlated).
Each latent variable needs a scale, set by fixing one loading to 1 or fixing the factor variance to 1.
Identification matters. Constructs with several indicators are more stable, and a minimum of about three indicators per factor is a common guideline (two can work when factors are correlated). 
Because the measurement model has no structural constraints among constructs, it serves as a baseline for later structural tests.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
3.3 Assessment of Fit

Overall fit

The chi-square test compares the model-implied and observed covariance matrices. It is very sensitive to sample size, so a significant chi-square in a large sample does not by itself mean the model is unusable.
The authors therefore recommend supplementing it with incremental fit indices, which compare the model against a baseline (null) model. Examples include the Bentler-Bonett normed fit index and the Tucker-Lewis index. 

Component (local) fit

Overall fit can hide local problems, so individual parameters and residuals must be inspected.
Look at the size and significance of the loadings, standardized residuals, error variances, and the reliability of the indicators and constructs.

Convergent validity is supported when the loadings of a construct’s indicators are large and statistically significant.
Discriminant validity is commonly assessed pairwise.

Compare the freely estimated model against one where the correlation between two constructs is fixed to 1, using a chi-square difference test.
A significantly better fit for the free model supports the claim that the two constructs are distinct.
Confidence intervals around the factor correlation that exclude 1 give similar evidence.

Fit should be judged with several sources of evidence together, not one index or cutoff.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
3.4 Respecification

When the measurement model fits poorly, researchers may revise it, but the changes should be principled.
Diagnostic tools include modification indices, standardized residuals, and expected parameter changes, which point to cross-loadings or correlated errors.
Preferred remedies are ones that preserve unidimensionality: dropping problematic indicators, or reassigning an indicator to a different construct when theory supports it. Freeing correlated errors or cross-loadings to force fit is discouraged.
Every change must have a substantive rationale, not just a statistical one.
Post hoc respecification is exploratory. Because it capitalizes on chance, the revised model should be cross-validated on an independent sample before being trusted.
Respecification should happen in the measurement step, before structural paths are examined, so measurement problems are not mistaken for structural ones.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
4.1 The Confirmatory Structural Model

The structural model specifies hypothesized relationships among latent constructs, such as directional paths, layered on top of the measurement model.
The full model therefore combines two parts: how indicators reflect constructs (measurement) and how constructs affect each other (structure).
Evaluating the structural model addresses nomological validity, meaning whether the relationships among constructs in the theoretical network behave as the theory predicts.
Structural models impose constraints on the factor relationships that the measurement model leaves free, so the measurement model is the least constrained comparison point for the structural model.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
4.2 Recommended Two-Step Modeling Approach
Step 1: Evaluate the measurement model

The measurement model represents how indicators relate to latent constructs, with the constructs freely correlated and no structural paths imposed.
It is evaluated separately so that problems with the indicators can be found and fixed without interference from the theory being tested.
Researchers learn whether the indicators are unidimensional, load meaningfully on their constructs (convergent validity), and distinguish one construct from another (discriminant validity).
If the fit is inadequate, researchers should check for weak, cross-loading, or misassigned indicators, consider principled respecification, and cross-validate. They should not move on to structural tests until measurement is acceptable.

Step 2: Evaluate the structural model

The structural model represents the hypothesized relationships among the latent constructs (paths, direct and indirect effects).
It differs from the measurement model in that it constrains how constructs relate, whereas the measurement model lets all of them correlate freely.
It should be evaluated only after acceptable measurement is established, because structural estimates are only meaningful if the constructs are measured well.
The structural model’s fit is assessed against the measurement model (the least constrained version), which isolates how much fit is lost by imposing the theory. This step contributes evidence for nomological validity.

Nested models and sequential chi-square difference tests

The authors use a sequence of nested models to compare the theoretical model with more and less constrained alternatives.

The theoretical model of interest is compared with a slightly more constrained model and a slightly less constrained model.
The measurement model can be viewed as a fully saturated structural model, giving the best-fitting reference point.

Sequential chi-square difference tests (SCDTs) evaluate these comparisons step by step, so each test speaks to a specific set of constraints.
The intent is to show whether the theoretical structure is adequate and whether omitted or unnecessary paths are present, rather than relying on one overall fit statistic.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
text:
4.3 Advantages of the Two-Step Approach

Locating the source of poor fit. If the measurement model fits but the structural model does not, the problem is in the theory. If the measurement model itself is poor, the indicators need work.
Preventing masking. Good fit in one component (for example, a well-specified measurement part) can hide problems in another when everything is estimated at once. Separating the steps reduces this.
Avoiding interpretational confounding. In a one-step approach, the empirical meaning of a construct can shift depending on the structural paths, because the loadings adjust to the structure. A stable measurement model prevents the meaning of constructs from changing with the theory being tested. Large differences in loadings between the two steps are a warning sign.
Supporting meaningful comparison of alternative models. When measurement is stable, competing structural theories can be compared on the same measures, so differences in fit reflect theory rather than shifting measurement.
Overall, the approach improves clarity, diagnosis, and confidence in theoretical conclusions.

title: SEM01 Take Notes for Anderson and Gerbing
section: 4.4 Additional Considerations in Structural Model Interpretation
text:
4.4 Additional Considerations in Structural Model Interpretation

Adequate fit does not prove that a model is correct. It only shows the model is not contradicted by the data, and other models may fit equally well (equivalent models).
Structural respecification carries the same risk as measurement respecification: capitalizing on chance and drifting into exploratory use.
Modifications should be theory-driven and, whenever possible, cross-validated on new data.
Causal interpretation requires more than good fit, since design, theory, and temporal ordering also matter.
Results should be reported with modest, careful conclusions that acknowledge alternative explanations.
